papers.summary: Based on the analysis of 96 organizational innovation in healthcare (OIH) projects and 52 interviews conducted with project leaders initiating these innovations, this research identifies the phenomena underlying the genesis of OIHs. The results highlight the major role played by factors such as patient empathy, international inspiration, academic inspiration, technological inspiration, serendipitous encounters, and the desire for organizational transformation in driving the generation of OIHs. Furthermore, our findings emphasize the dual nature of the research and development process for these innovations, characterized as both ex nihilo and ex materia.

papers.title: A collaborative and participatory approach to public service innovation: Health sector dynamics and outlook
papers.title_ja: 公共医療サービスイノベーションへの協働的参加的アプローチ：保健部門のダイナミクスと展望
papers.authors: Fatima Yatim, Alan Sitkin, Cadenza Academic Translations
papers.summary: This article explores the dynamics of collaborative and participatory innovations in public health services using Chen et al.’s (2020) typology. Based on a mixed survey of projects awarded under the national “Droits des usagers de la santé” initiative, the study finds that user participation primarily generates operational and capacity-oriented innovations frequently involving external partnerships. The analysis highlights the crucial interactions between internal and external dynamics, identifying essential conditions for successful innovations: effective mobilization of internal resources, robust institutional support, and early and active user involvement. However, the study also identifies limitations in citizen engagement, particularly in the evaluation phase of innovations. The article concludes by suggesting avenues for enhancing full co-creation processes in public services to maximize public value.

papers.summary: The Book of Architecture of John Thorpe (c.1565-1655) consists of some 295 drawings ranging primarily from the 1590s to the 1620s and covering 168 buildings, mainly but not only English, and amongst the greatest of the period. The drawings include plans, elevations, some full-size sections of mouldings, and a depiction of the five orders derived from Hans Blum’s 1550 treatise on the orders. Bound in a hard cover in the 18th c., since 1810 the album has been preserved in one of London’s most iconic museums of British architecture, created by the celebrated architect Sir John Soane (1753-1837), who added to the album with about six sketches of his own. Alongside new catalogue entries featuring digital copies of the drawings in colour, enlargeable, and uncut, my edition will include a c.40.000-word critical analysis addressing all aspects above-mentioned. papers.summary: The Routledge Companion to Global Art Histories brings together new scholarship on the methods, materials and institutional conditions through which art history is being rethought beyond inherited Euro-American narratives. Rather than treating the global as a matter of expanded coverage, the volume approaches global art histories as a set of relations: between works of art and their conditions of appearance; between archives, publics and institutions; between pedagogy and disciplinary formation; and between artistic practice and the political, ecological and historical pressures that shape its interpretation. Edited by Diana Newall, Grant Pooke and Leon Wainwright, the book includes substantial editorial material: a general introduction, four section introductions and a coda, ‘Against the Comfort of Critique’. papers.summary: Chopin adhered to traditional practices in musical form to a far greater extent than hitherto acknowledged. He took certain standard formal paths with remarkable consistency throughout his compositional career and across almost all his favoured genres. His choices were grounded in eighteenth-century routines concerning intrathematic functions and schemata. Chopin pursued alterations and adaptations of those formal patterns, resulting in a kaleidoscopic range of variants, and in this way presented his compositions in a guise amenable to Romantic taste. papers.summary: In this transformative study, Simon Smith explores how playwrights like Shakespeare crafted their plays for demanding and varied commercial audiences. Rediscovering the many forms of judgement practiced in the early modern playhouse, he investigates influences ranging from the classical tradition and grammar-school classroom to ballad and jest culture. Where many prior studies have treated 'the judicious' as a self-contained subset of playgoers, Smith reveals the variety of careful assessments made in the theatre by a wide range of playgoers, showing that judgement and pleasure were often simultaneous elements of the same response. Chapters examine specific parts of plays that were especially subject to evaluation and generative of enjoyment: spectacle, words, plot, and actorly technique. papers.summary: This chapter examines the creative and theoretical tensions that emerge when postdigital fiction authors collaborate with large language models (LLMs) trained on hegemonic discourse and structures. LLMs, designed primarily by and for dominant (cis-het white male, American corporate) perspectives, internalize and reproduce these patriarchal structures in their textual outputs. papers.title: All Agnes Wants is the Green of a Forest:The Dialectics of Interconnectedness and Grief in Hamnet
papers.title_ja: アグネスの望むもの：森の緑—『ハムネット』における相互連結性と悲しみの弁証法
papers.summary: Treating novel and film as thesis and antithesis, this chapter draws out ideas about breath in the novel and explores their transfer to the screen. It therefore seeks evidence of synthesis in how Zhao elicits meaning from camera movement and editing, choral music and breathing sounds, and a juxtaposition of close-ups with deep-focus wide and long shots that both simulates and stimulates breathing. Consequently, this analysis reinforces the theme of interconnectedness by consideration of the adaptation process as an exchange of energy between the novel and the film, by tracking descriptions of breathing in the novel and following this by analysing corresponding scenes in the film. Finally, this chapter explores how the link between ancient Daoist traditions of meditation and universal experiences of grief provides evidence of Zhao as an atemporal, transnational, peripatetic filmmaker.
